newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary government approves 1997 draft budget.
newsitem.headline: Hungary government approves 1997 draft budget.

text.p: The Hungarian government approved the draft 1997 budget and decided to cut state expenditures by 10 billion forints ($63.52 million) this year, Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy announced on Thursday.

According to the draft, which is to be submitted to Parliament on Monday, Hungary plans to reduce inflation and the budget deficit, and widen the base of social security contributions, Medgyessy told a news conference.
Hungary plans to push average annual inflation down to 18 percent next year, compared with the latest official forecast of 22 to 24 percent for 1996.

The country targets a general government deficit of 390 billion forints, or 4.9 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) for next year, which is not comparable to this year's four percent projection as the accounting system of the state debt will change from 1997, Medgyessy said.

"In a comparative structure, (the 4.9 percent) corresponds to three percent," the minister told a conference of local municipalities on Wednesday, adding that the change was technical and did not demand economic policy action.

The planned accounting change means that the devaluation losses on Hungary's foreign state debt will appear in the state budget from next year, instead of the National Bank of Hungary's books as to the current practice.

Budget expenditures will be curbed by increasing subsidies to state agencies by only 15 percent and to local municipalities by 13 percent in 1997, compared with the 18 percent inflation target, Medgyessy said.

Hungary will begin the reform of social security contributions in 1997 so as to break the social security budget even next year, he said, adding that the latest offical forecast for the 1996 social security deficit for 1996 was 53 billion forints.
This was up from the 17.8 billion original target and some 40 billion forints in 1995.
Medgyessy said the government decided to save 10 billion forints from this year's central state budget expenditures to plug the gap of the social security funds.

With the cuts, which will affect state agencies, Hungary expects to keep the deficit of the general government, including the central budget and state funds, at four percent of the GDP as agreed with the International Monetary Fund.
Hungary plans to widen next year the field of those revenues upon which social security contribution is paid and introduce a minimum social security contribution.
Revenues will be increased by these measures, and that enables Hungary to reduce social security contributions paid by employers to 41 percent from the current 42.5 percent, Medgyessy said.
He added the cut was smaller than the previously planned 2.5 percent, but from July 1997 the government will introduce further reduction if the state of the social security budget justifies that.

The registration system of the healthcare fund will be modernized from a World Bank loan and 1.2 billion forints to be provided by the state, and the government expects the fund to tighten control on revenue collection, Medgyessy said.
